The required integers are exactly
\[
\boxed{n\equiv 0 \text{ or } 1 \pmod 4,\quad n\ge 2.}
\]

Let \(\left(\frac ab\right)\) denote the Legendre symbol. Since every \(p_i\equiv 3\pmod4\), quadratic reciprocity gives, for \(i\ne j\),
\[
\left(\frac{p_i}{p_j}\right)\left(\frac{p_j}{p_i}\right)=-1.
\]

The condition is
\[
\prod_{i\ne j}\left(\frac{p_i}{p_j}\right)=1
\]
for every \(j\). Multiplying these \(n\) equations over all \(j\), the left side factors over unordered pairs:
\[
1=\prod_{j=1}^n\prod_{i\ne j}\left(\frac{p_i}{p_j}\right)
=\prod_{1\le i<j\le n}
\left(\frac{p_i}{p_j}\right)\left(\frac{p_j}{p_i}\right)
=(-1)^{\binom n2}.
\]
Thus \(\binom n2\) must be even, i.e.
\[
\frac{n(n-1)}2\equiv0\pmod2,
\]
which is equivalent to
\[
n\equiv0 \text{ or }1\pmod4.
\]

It remains to prove sufficiency.

We first choose signs \(\varepsilon_{ij}\in\{\pm1\}\) for \(i\ne j\) such that
\[
\varepsilon_{ij}=-\varepsilon_{ji}
\qquad\text{and}\qquad
\prod_{i\ne j}\varepsilon_{ij}=1
\]
for every \(j\). This is the same as orienting the complete graph \(K_n\) so that every vertex has even indegree: put \(\varepsilon_{ij}=-1\) exactly when the edge is oriented \(i\to j\).

Such an orientation exists precisely when \(\binom n2\) is even.

For \(n\equiv1\pmod4\), use the regular cyclic tournament: label vertices modulo \(n\), and orient \(x\to y\) when
\[
y-x\in\{1,2,\dots,(n-1)/2\}.
\]
Each vertex has indegree \((n-1)/2\), which is even.

For \(n\equiv0\pmod4\), let vertex \(0\) point to every other vertex. On the remaining \(n-1\) vertices, use the regular cyclic tournament. Each remaining vertex has internal indegree
\[
\frac{n-2}{2},
\]
which is odd, and receives one additional edge from vertex \(0\), so its total indegree is even. Vertex \(0\) has indegree \(0\).

Now we realize these signs by primes. We claim that for any such antisymmetric sign pattern \(\varepsilon_{ij}\), there exist distinct primes \(p_1,\dots,p_n\equiv3\pmod4\) such that
\[
\left(\frac{p_i}{p_j}\right)=\varepsilon_{ij}.
\]

Construct them inductively. Suppose \(p_1,\dots,p_k\) have already been chosen. To choose \(p_{k+1}\), pick a residue class \(r\pmod{4p_1\cdots p_k}\) satisfying
\[
r\equiv3\pmod4
\]
and, for each \(j\le k\),
\[
\left(\frac r{p_j}\right)=\varepsilon_{k+1,j}.
\]
This is possible by the Chinese remainder theorem, since modulo each \(p_j\) we may choose either a quadratic residue or a nonresidue as required. By Dirichlet’s theorem on primes in arithmetic progressions, there is a prime
\[
p_{k+1}\equiv r\pmod{4p_1\cdots p_k}.
\]
Then \(p_{k+1}\equiv3\pmod4\), and
\[
\left(\frac{p_{k+1}}{p_j}\right)=\varepsilon_{k+1,j}.
\]
Because both primes are \(3\pmod4\), quadratic reciprocity gives
\[
\left(\frac{p_j}{p_{k+1}}\right)
=-\left(\frac{p_{k+1}}{p_j}\right)
=\varepsilon_{j,k+1}.
\]
Thus the construction continues.

Finally, for each \(j\),
\[
\left(\frac{\prod_{i\ne j}p_i}{p_j}\right)
=\prod_{i\ne j}\left(\frac{p_i}{p_j}\right)
=\prod_{i\ne j}\varepsilon_{ij}
=1,
\]
so the required product is a quadratic residue modulo \(p_j\).

Therefore the exact set of integers is
\[
\boxed{\{\,n\ge2:\ n\equiv0\text{ or }1\pmod4\,\}}.
\]
